item.title: Larch Season: The Two Weeks the Valley Turns Gold
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Western larch drops its needles instead of keeping them, and for a short window each fall the drainages around the Flathead go gold. Where it happens, roughly when it peaks, and why the timing shifts with elevation.
item.content:encoded:
Larch Season: The Two Weeks the Valley Turns Gold

Most people move to the Flathead for the summers. A fair number of them decide to stay because of two weeks in the fall they never saw coming.

Western larch — locals call it tamarack — is a conifer that does something conifers aren't supposed to do: it drops its needles. Every other evergreen on the mountainside holds green through the winter. The larch turns gold first, then rust, then bare, and for a short stretch every year whole drainages around this valley light up in a way that catches newcomers completely off guard. Nobody tells them to look up. They find out by accident, usually driving somewhere else.

Here's what that window actually looks like, where to see it, and what it has to do with whether you'd actually want to live here.

What You're Looking At

A larch isn't dying when it turns — it's doing what it does every single year. The needles go through a genuine color change: green to a soft yellow, then a deeper gold, then almost orange-rust right before they let go entirely. Because larch tends to grow in dense stands mixed among the true evergreens, the effect isn't one tree turning color — it's whole hillsides of gold set against the dark green of the Douglas fir and lodgepole that never change at all. From a distance it reads less like fall foliage and more like the mountain got lit from inside.

It's a different kind of color season than what most people picture when they think "autumn in the mountains." There's no red, almost no orange until the very end, and it doesn't happen on a deciduous tree in a yard — it happens on a conifer, on a slope, at a distance. That's exactly why it surprises people who moved here expecting Vermont and got something else entirely.

When It Peaks — and Why the Window Moves

The honest answer is that there isn't one fixed date, because elevation runs the calendar here more than the calendar does. Higher stands typically turn first, working down toward the valley floor as the weeks go on, which is why the color seems to migrate downhill through the season instead of happening everywhere at once. In a typical year that means the change gets underway in the second half of September at elevation and builds toward a broader, valley-wide peak sometime in the back half of October, occasionally stretching toward the start of November in a mild year. An early hard frost can compress the whole window; a warm, dry stretch can stretch it out. The only reliable rule is to watch the higher drainages first — if they're turning, the lower country is a couple of weeks behind.

Where to Go Look

You don't need a permit or a plan, just a direction to point the truck.

The Hungry Horse Reservoir area, up the South Fork past Columbia Falls, is some of the most reliable tamarack country in the valley — dense stands, big water, and far fewer people on a random Tuesday than Flathead Lake sees on a summer Saturday. The Middle Fork of the Flathead, where it runs alongside US-2 toward Glacier's southern boundary, puts you in larch country with almost no effort — it's a highway view, not a hike. For something closer to town, Herron Park on Kalispell's edge and the Rails to Trails corridor give you the color on a lunchtime walk. Further out, the Seeley-Swan valley and the North Fork Road toward Polebridge both run through heavy larch country, though the North Fork is unpaved and washboarded by this time of year — worth the trip, not worth doing on a schedule.

None of this requires Glacier Park itself, though the park's lower-elevation corridors carry their share of larch too, especially along the Middle Fork side. If you're headed that way, plan around the season change: the alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road closes with the first serious snow, typically before larch season fully wraps up, so check conditions before you commit a whole day to it.

What It Has to Do With Buying a House Here

I bring this up every fall for the same reason: it's the season that tells you whether you actually like it here, or just liked visiting in July.

A house that gets shown in June photographs beautifully and tells you almost nothing about what the property feels like the other nine months of the year. Larch season is a decent stand-in test. If you can picture yourself driving up the South Fork on a random Tuesday afternoon just to see the color change — not because you have to, just because you want to — that's a different kind of buyer than someone who's only ever pictured the dock in August. Both are fine reasons to be here. They just point toward different parts of the valley, and toward a very different conversation about what you're actually buying.

This isn't a pitch to buy in October. It's a suggestion: if you're seriously weighing a move to the Flathead, come back and drive it once the green thins out. The place you fall for in a fall storm of gold needles is the same one you'll be living in come February — and it's worth knowing which version you actually signed up for.

item.title: The Empty House in Winter: Protecting an Inherited Home Until It Sells
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Probate runs longer than the season does. What a family needs handled before the first hard freeze so an inherited Flathead home doesn't lose real money sitting vacant.
item.content:encoded:
The Empty House in Winter: Protecting an Inherited Home Until It Sells

Probate has its own calendar, and it rarely lines up with the one on the wall.

By the time an estate clears the paperwork, secures the personal representative's authority, and gets a house ready to list, it's not unusual for a Flathead property to sit empty through its first winter with nobody living in it. Nobody plans for that. It just happens — the legal side takes the time it takes, and the house sits there in the meantime, unattended, while temperatures do what they do in this valley from November through March.

An empty house doesn't fail all at once. It fails quietly, in ways nobody notices until spring, when the family walks in for a showing and finds out what a Flathead winter did to a place with no one watching it.

If you're a personal representative or an heir looking at a vacant house and a first freeze on the calendar, here's what actually needs handling — the practical care of an asset the family is holding on someone else's behalf, not the legal side, which is your attorney's to walk you through.

Call the insurer before you call anyone else

This is the one people skip, and it's the one that costs the most when they do.

A standard homeowners policy is written for an occupied house. Most carriers have a vacancy clause that limits or excludes coverage — water damage in particular — once a home sits empty past a stated number of consecutive days, often 30 to 60 depending on the policy. If a pipe freezes and bursts in an unoccupied house and the insurer can show the vacancy exclusion applied, the estate can be looking at a claim that pays little or nothing on exactly the kind of loss an empty winter house is most exposed to.

Tell the carrier the home is vacant, in writing, the day it becomes vacant. Ask directly whether the existing policy still covers it, whether a vacant-home endorsement or a separate vacant-property policy is needed, and what conditions that coverage requires — a working heat source above a minimum temperature is a common one. This is a conversation for the estate's attorney and the insurer, not a guess on my end, but it needs to happen before the first hard freeze, not after a claim.

Heat, water, and the pipes in between

Once coverage is sorted, the mechanical decision is heat left on versus the system drained. Both work; picking neither is what causes damage.

Left occupied-style, most guidance is to keep the thermostat no lower than the mid-50s, which keeps interior wall cavities above freezing without running a full heating bill on an empty house. The alternative is a full drain-down: water shut off at the main, lines blown out or drained, and antifreeze in traps and toilets — done properly, usually by a plumber, so nothing gets missed. A house that's heated but has water shut off and lines drained anyway is the safest combination, since a frozen pipe with no water behind it does far less damage than one that's pressurized.

Either way, pay attention to the pipes on exterior walls and in unheated spaces — garages, crawl spaces, an addition with thinner insulation — since those freeze first regardless of what the thermostat says. And don't forget the water heater; draining it or leaving it running is its own decision, not an afterthought to the rest of the system.

Snow, ice, and a house that doesn't look empty

An inherited home still needs a driveway a plow can reach and a roofline that isn't building an ice dam over the gutters. Arrange snow removal on a standing schedule, not a call-when-someone-remembers basis — both so the house stays passable for showings once it's ready to list, and because an unplowed drive and an unshoveled walk are the fastest visual signal to a passerby that nobody's home.

Ice damming is worth a specific mention: heat escaping through an under-insulated attic melts snow on the roof, it refreezes at the colder eave, and water backs up under the shingles into the house. It's a slow, expensive kind of damage that shows up as a stain on a ceiling months later. A quick check of attic insulation and gutter clearing before the snow starts is cheap compared to what a winter of damming can do.

A set of eyes, on a schedule

Mail piling up in a box, a light that's never on, snow that never gets tracked — these are the details that tell the wrong kind of visitor a house is unattended. Arrange for someone — a neighbor, a property-watch service, or a local contact — to physically check the house on a regular schedule through the winter: confirm heat is holding, look for water, collect mail, and make sure the place reads as looked-after even when it isn't lived in.

The part worth saying out loud

None of this is legal work. It's the maintenance an estate has to fund and coordinate to protect an asset that isn't anyone's home anymore but still belongs to the family until it sells. Skipping it doesn't save money — it just moves the cost from a manageable winter bill to a spring repair, right when the house needs to show well.

So the question worth asking before the first hard freeze: does this house have a plan for the next four months, or does it just have an address?

item.title: What You Sign Before You Tour: Buyer Agency in Montana
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Montana buyers now sign a written agreement before seeing the inside of a house. Here's what that document actually sets, and how to hold someone to it.
item.content:encoded:
What You Sign Before You Tour: Buyer Agency in Montana

Most buyers sign it on a doorstep. Phone in one hand, agent's tablet in the other, ninety seconds before the first showing of the day — and most of them don't read a line of it before they do.

That's the buyer representation agreement, and since the nationwide practice changes that followed the 2024 NAR settlement, it's not optional paperwork anymore. If you want an agent to walk you through a house that's listed with a Montana Regional MLS participant, you sign one first. So if you're about to start touring Kalispell or Whitefish homes and someone hands you a form before you've seen a single closet, here's what it actually says — and what to look at before your name goes on it.

The Document at the Door

A buyer representation agreement is a written contract between you and a real estate agent (or the agent's brokerage) that spells out the working relationship before any house-hunting starts. It's the buyer-side mirror of the listing agreement a seller signs with their agent. Neither is new in concept — what changed in 2024 is that it's now required in writing, signed, before a buyer's agent can tour a property with you.

That's a reasonable thing to require. A written scope of work is how you hold someone to a standard — what they're doing for you, how long, and on what terms. The problem isn't the requirement. The problem is signing it at the door without understanding what's in it.

Term and Exclusivity: What You're Actually Agreeing To

Two questions matter more than the rest of the page combined.

How long does it run? Some agreements run 90 days, some run a year. If this is your first time working with an agent, there's no reason to sign anything longer than a single showing or a short trial window — 30 days is common and reasonable to ask for. You can always extend it once you know the agent is a fit. Locking into a long term before the first tour is backwards.

Is it exclusive? An exclusive agreement means that agent represents you for the term, full stop — even if you stumble across a house on your own, at an open house, or through a friend's listing. A non-exclusive agreement lets you work with more than one agent at a time. Most buyers don't need multiple agents; they need to know which kind they signed. If you find a for-sale-by-owner or a new-construction spec home on a Sunday drive while under an exclusive agreement, that agent may still be owed a role — or a fee — depending on how the form is written. Ask before it happens, not after.

Scope and Compensation

The agreement also sets the territory: one specific property, a single town, or the whole Flathead Valley. If you're not sure yet whether you're buying in Kalispell proper or looking as far out as Columbia Falls or Bigfork, don't sign something that boxes you into one zip code before you've decided.

Then there's the part that changed the most in the last two years: how the agent gets paid, and who pays it. Buyer-agent compensation is no longer something that gets quietly handled through the MLS listing. The agreement states a specific number or percentage, and it states who's expected to pay it — the seller (through the offer), the buyer directly, or some combination negotiated deal by deal. None of that is fixed by law or by MLS rule anymore. It's a line in the document you're signing, and it's negotiable. Read it, and if the number doesn't match what you expected going in, ask about it before you're three showings deep.

The Protection Period

Most agreements include a protection period — a window, often 30 to 90 days after the agreement ends, during which the agent is still owed compensation if you buy a home they introduced you to or showed you during the term. This exists so an agent who does the work of showing you fifteen houses isn't cut out of the deal because you waited three weeks to make an offer. It's standard, and it's fair in principle. What matters is knowing the window exists and roughly how long it runs, so there's no surprise if you go back to a house you saw with one agent after you've started working with another.

If It Isn't Working

A buyer agreement isn't a life sentence. If the relationship isn't working — slow communication, a mismatch in how you search, an agent who isn't showing up prepared — most agreements have a cancellation path, and a good agent won't make you fight for it. Ask what that path looks like before you sign, not after you're frustrated. If it isn't spelled out, ask directly: "If this isn't a fit, how do we end it?" The answer to that question tells you a lot about who you're about to spend the next few months with.

None of this is a hurdle standing between you and the house you want. It's the tool that makes sure the person walking you through it is actually working for you, on terms you both agreed to and can both point back to. Read it before you sign it, ask the questions above, and the rest of the search gets a lot simpler.

This post explains general practice and is not legal advice. Buyer agency forms vary by brokerage — review the specific agreement you're asked to sign, and consult an attorney if you have questions about its terms.

item.title: Showings While You're Both Still Living There
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Neither of you has moved out yet, and the house is already listed. Here's how a showing schedule actually gets built — one calendar, confirmed appointments, and a plan for the kids — when two people who'd rather not coordinate directly still have to share a front door.
item.content:encoded:
Showings While You're Both Still Living There

The house is listed. Neither of you has moved out yet.

That's the month nobody plans for when a Flathead Valley divorce sale gets underway. Everyone braces for the closing table. Almost nobody braces for Tuesday at 4pm, when a buyer's agent wants to walk through the kitchen and both names on the deed are still sleeping under the same roof.

If you're wondering how other people get through this part without it becoming the worst month of the whole process, here's what actually works.

One calendar, not two phones

The single biggest mistake I see is treating showings like any other logistics question between two people who are separating — handled by text, in the moment, back and forth.

That works fine for deciding who picks up milk. It does not work for a stream of showing requests coming in from agents who don't know your situation and don't need to. Every request that lands in a group text becomes a small negotiation, and a house going through a divorce sale generates a lot of small negotiations before it generates a closing.

The fix is boring on purpose: one written calendar, one place, both of you can see it without asking the other person anything. I set this up before the sign goes in the yard, not after the first awkward showing. Requests come to me, I check it against the calendar, I confirm or propose an alternate time, and both of you get the same notice at the same time. Neither of you is coordinating with the other directly, and neither of you is finding out about a showing from a lockbox log.

Confirmed appointments only, and why that lowers the temperature

A house that's simply "available anytime" sounds convenient. In a situation like this, it's the opposite — it means either party can be caught off guard, which turns every doorbell into a small conflict.

Confirmed-appointments-only changes that. A showing isn't a showing until it's on the calendar and both parties have had the agreed notice window to prepare. No surprise walk-throughs, no "the agent said it would just be five minutes." That one rule removes most of the friction before it starts, because nobody is ever wondering whether someone might show up unannounced.

The kids' schedule sets the boundaries, not the buyer's

Buyers' schedules are flexible. A ten-year-old's school pickup is not. I build the showing windows around the school run and activities first, and everything else gets scheduled inside what's left — evenings after the bus, weekend blocks that don't collide with practices or the other parent's time. A buyer's agent asking for a Tuesday-at-3pm slot doesn't get to override that just because it's the only opening in their calendar; there's almost always another time that works, and it's my job to find it rather than yours.

Securing what shouldn't be part of the showing

A house that's occupied by two people mid-divorce usually has things sitting out that have nothing to do with selling it — financial documents, mail, medication, jewelry, anything either of you wouldn't want a stranger picking up off a dresser. Strangers walking through your home is already uncomfortable. It shouldn't also be a security risk.

Before the first showing, we walk the house together — or separately, whichever you prefer — and agree on where personal papers and valuables get secured for the duration of the listing. A lockable filing box in a closet, not spread across a desk. This is a five-minute conversation up front that saves a much worse one later.

Whose job it is to have the house ready

This is the question that causes the most friction, and it's worth answering explicitly rather than assuming. If one of you is home more, or one of you cares more about how the house shows, that's fine — but it should be agreed, not defaulted into. I put it in writing at listing: who's responsible for the house being presentable on a scheduled showing day, and what "presentable" means, so it isn't relitigated every week.

When one person starts declining showings

Sometimes a person who agreed to all of this at the start starts saying no to individual requests a few weeks in. Before assuming that's bad faith, it's worth asking why — a bad week, a scheduling conflict, or genuine discomfort with the pace. My job stays the same either way: keep both attorneys and both of you informed, document every request and every response in writing, and let that record speak for itself if it ever needs to. A documented process is a calm process, and staying neutral is what lets me keep working the file for both of you.

A question worth sitting with

If a buyer's agent called right now asking for a showing tomorrow at 5pm, would you know — without a single text to your ex — whether that works?

If the answer is no, that's the gap worth closing before the first showing request comes in, not after.

item.title: Ask Versus Close: What Flathead Sellers Are Actually Getting
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Every seller watches the list price. Almost none watch the gap between what a house asks and what it actually closes at — and right now in the Flathead, that gap is where the real story is.
item.content:encoded:
Every seller in the Flathead Valley can quote their neighbor's list price from memory. Almost nobody can tell you what that house actually closed at, or how many times the number changed between the sign going up and the sale going final.

That's backwards. The list price is a guess. The close price is the truth. And the spread between the two — plus how many times a seller had to move the ask to get there — is the single clearest read on where this market actually sits right now.

Numbers first, then what to do with them.

The Numbers: Mid-August Through Mid-September

For Kalispell, the period August 13 through September 13, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, that period):

  • Active listings: 503, up 2.03% from the prior month
  • New listings: 104
  • Average asking price on active listings: $953,000 — down 10.24% from the prior month
  • Average original list price on that same pool: roughly $968,000
  • Price reductions: 141 listings, up sharply and now representing better than one in four active listings
  • Average days on market: 115.84 days, up 3.43%

Separately, Montana Regional MLS figures reported through Movoto put Kalispell's median closed sale price at $699,000 for August 2026, with median days on market at 77 — up from 62 days a year ago.

On rates: Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.76% as of September 10, 2026, up slightly from 6.71% the week before.

A clean, published original-list-to-final-close ratio isn't available for this market this month — the MLS feeds that would produce it don't break it out publicly at the county level. But the two things that stand in for it, the reduction rate and the days-on-market trend, are telling the same story from two different directions, and it's worth reading them together instead of picking whichever one is more comfortable.

What the Reduction Rate Is Actually Telling You

More than one in four active Kalispell listings has already had at least one price cut. That's not a handful of overpriced outliers — that's a market-wide signal. When a quarter of the inventory needs a correction to keep moving, the problem isn't a few sellers who got greedy. It's that the starting assumption a lot of listings were priced against — where the market was a few months ago — has already moved on by the time the sign goes in the yard.

The average asking price on active listings has fallen roughly 10% in a single month, from an original average list closer to $968,000 down to $953,000 now showing. Some of that is new, more realistically priced inventory coming on. A meaningful piece of it is existing listings getting corrected because the first number didn't work.

Either way, the direction is the same: sellers are giving ground after listing, not before. That's the expensive way to find the right price.

Days on Market Is the Other Half of the Story

Average days on market sitting at 115.84 days — and separately, median days on market up to 77 from 62 a year ago — both point the same direction. Homes are taking longer to move than they were twelve months ago, and every extra week a listing sits is a week where a buyer sees the "days on market" counter climbing on the listing page and starts wondering what's wrong with the house rather than what's wrong with the price.

That's the mechanism worth understanding: a stale listing doesn't just wait for the right buyer. It actively signals something to every buyer who scrolls past it. By the time a seller finally cuts the price to where it should have started, they're often negotiating against their own listing history, not just the market.

What This Means If You're Pricing Right Now

If you're getting ready to list, the question isn't "what did the house down the street ask for." It's "what did the house down the street actually close at, and how many cuts did it take to get there." That number exists — your agent can pull it from sold comps — and it's a far better anchor than any asking price still sitting active on the market.

If you're already listed and haven't had a single showing in three weeks, the reduction-rate math above should tell you something: more than a quarter of your competition has already adjusted. Waiting to be the last one to move is not a strategy, it's a cost, measured in the extra days-on-market number that follows the listing around.

The sellers doing well in this market right now aren't the ones who priced highest. They're the ones who priced against where the market actually is today, took the showings that came in the first two weeks seriously as real feedback, and made one clean adjustment early instead of three small ones late.

If you're wondering whether your number is priced against last month's market or this one, that's worth a direct conversation before the listing goes live — not after it's been sitting for ten weeks.

item.title: The Plan You Hope You Never Open
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Every solid operation has a primary plan and a contingency, and the contingency gets written before anyone needs it. Here's how that habit applies to a real estate transaction — and why clients feel the difference when it does.
item.content:encoded:
Every transaction has two versions of what happens next. There's the one everybody's hoping for — clean appraisal, clean inspection, financing clears on schedule, keys change hands on the date printed on the contract. And there's the other one, the one nobody wants to talk about at the kitchen table: the appraisal comes in short, the buyer's financing falls apart with ten days left, the inspector finds something behind a wall nobody knew was there.

Most people only plan for the first version. That's backwards.

The Habit That Doesn't Come From Real Estate

Before any operation, there's a primary plan and there's a contingency — and the contingency doesn't get written in the middle of the crisis it's meant to solve. It gets written before anyone steps off, while everyone's calm and thinking clearly, precisely because that's the only time anyone thinks clearly. By the time something actually goes wrong, the plan already exists. Nobody's inventing a response under pressure. They're just executing the next page.

That habit doesn't turn off when the work changes. It shows up now in how a file gets prepared before a client ever asks a question, in how comps get run before they're needed rather than after, and in the fact that a contingency for the deal already exists before the deal needs one. It's not a personality quirk. It's a service standard — the same one that got applied under considerably higher stakes, just aimed at a closing table instead.

What "Having a Plan" Actually Looks Like in a Transaction

Talk to enough agents and you'll hear a lot of confidence and not much specificity. Confidence isn't the same as a plan. A plan has to answer real questions, in advance, before anyone's emotional about the answer:

If the appraisal comes in short — is the buyer prepared to bring the difference in cash, is the seller open to a partial price adjustment, or does the contract get renegotiated? That conversation should happen before an appraiser ever sets foot on the property, not after the number lands and everyone's scrambling.

If financing falls apart late — what's the buyer's backup lender, how fast can they actually move, and at what point does the seller need to know the listing might need to go back on the market? Ten days from closing is not when you want to be asking these questions for the first time.

If the inspection turns up something structural — is there already a sense of what repairs the seller will negotiate versus walk away from, and does the buyer have a number in mind for what changes the deal versus what they can live with? A pre-decided range keeps a hard conversation from turning into a stalled one.

If the buyer's own sale collapses — was there ever a contingency built around it in the first place, and if not, what's the fallback timeline everyone agreed to going in?

None of these are exotic. Every experienced agent has seen versions of all four. The difference isn't whether the scenario gets anticipated — it's whether it got discussed on a calm Tuesday afternoon or discovered on a panicked Thursday night with a closing date bearing down.

Why This Matters More Than It Sounds Like It Should

Here's the part that actually changes the client experience: when something does go sideways — and across enough transactions, something eventually does — the call that delivers the bad news is not the same call that leaves someone standing there with no idea what happens next. If the contingency was built ahead of time, that same phone call also delivers the next three steps. The client hears "here's what happened, and here's exactly what we do now" in the same breath.

Compare that to the alternative: the news lands, and now everyone's improvising a response to a problem that could have been anticipated a month earlier. That's where transactions actually fall apart — not usually because the underlying problem was unsolvable, but because nobody had a plan when it showed up, and improvised decisions under pressure are rarely anyone's best ones.

Panic, in a real estate transaction, is almost always a planning failure. It is not a personality failure, and it's not bad luck. It's a gap that existed before the stressful moment ever arrived, and it was closeable in advance.

What This Looks Like Working With Ryan

This isn't a pitch for pessimism, and it's not about assuming every deal is headed for trouble — most aren't. It's about treating a transaction the way any serious plan gets treated: build the primary path, and build the fallback before you need it, so that if the day comes, there's already an answer instead of a scramble.

Buyers and sellers in the Flathead Valley get that same approach applied to their file from day one — appraisal contingencies discussed up front, financing timelines built with slack instead of hope, inspection expectations set before the report ever arrives. Not because something is expected to go wrong, but because if it does, there's already a next step instead of a moment of silence on the phone.

If you're heading into a purchase or a sale and want to talk through what the contingency plan actually looks like for your situation — not the boilerplate version, the one built around your specific deal — that's a conversation worth having before you're under contract, not after.

item.title: The First Showing Happens on a Phone Screen
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Sellers spend weeks prepping the house and about four minutes thinking about the listing photos — which is backwards, because the photos decide whether anyone ever walks through the door. What Flathead Valley listing media actually needs, and how to judge a photographer before you hire one.
item.content:encoded:
How many buyers looked at your house this week and decided against it without you ever knowing they were there?

If the house is listed, the answer is dozens. Maybe hundreds. They looked at it on a phone — in a parking lot, in bed at eleven at night, on a couch in Spokane. Two to six seconds each. Then they kept scrolling.

That was the showing. The one with the lockbox and the shoes off at the door is the second showing, and few people ever get that far.

Sellers in Kalispell and Whitefish spend six weeks on the house and about four minutes on the media that represents it. It's backwards, and it's the most expensive inversion in the process.

The Photos Aren't a Record of the House. They Are the House.

Until a buyer is standing in your kitchen, the twenty-odd images in the listing are not a depiction of your property. They are your property. Every judgment gets made from them — price, condition, whether the floor plan works, whether it's worth the drive from Missoula on a Saturday.

This matters more here than in a lot of markets, because a meaningful share of Flathead buyers are not in the Flathead. They're relocating, buying a second home, or watching from two states away. They'll build a shortlist of four houses from photos alone and fly in for one weekend. You are either on that list or you aren't, and nothing about your granite or your new well pump enters into it.

Shoot Day Is the Real Deadline

Sellers set their sights on the list date. The date that matters is three or four days earlier, when the camera comes.

Everything has to be finished by then — not started, finished. The mulch down. The cars out of the driveway and off the street. The garbage cans gone, not tucked around the corner where the wide angle finds them anyway. Every light working, and every bulb the same color temperature — which sounds fussy until you see one room lit by three different whites.

You can keep improving the house after shoot day. The listing won't know. Whatever the camera sees is what the market sees for the whole run, and re-shoots almost never happen — by the time everyone agrees the photos are the problem, the listing is thirty days old and carrying that number around.

Wide Angle, and the Point Where It Becomes a Lie

There's a real line here and it's worth naming.

A properly wide lens is honest work. Rooms photograph smaller than they feel, and correcting for that is just competence. Push it further and you get the listing everyone in this valley has seen: a bedroom that appears to run forty feet, walls that bow at the edges, a bathroom where the vanity is somehow half a mile from the tub.

Those photos do get showings. Then the buyer walks in, feels the gap, and spends the rest of the tour wondering what else was oversold. You didn't gain a showing — you spent one, and some credibility with it.

The same applies to the twilight shot and the drone. Both earn their place — twilight for a house whose best feature is how it sits at dusk with the lights on, drone for anything where the land or the setting is a real part of the value. Twenty acres above the valley floor earns a drone shot. A quarter-acre in-town lot does not, and using one there mostly tells a buyer you're reaching.

What Fall Light Is Worth in January

It's mid-September. The grass is still green and the light is long and warm in the late afternoon. This is close to the best the valley photographs all year.

If there's any chance your house is still on the market in December, this is the argument for shooting now regardless of when you list. A house photographed in September and listed in November looks alive. The same house photographed in November looks like a house nobody wanted, which is a story the pictures tell whether it's true or not.

Floor Plans Cut the Showings You Don't Want

A simple measured floor plan is cheap, usually bundled with the shoot, and does what photos can't: it answers the layout question.

Buyers are quietly solving problems — will the piano fit, can the mother-in-law have a room on the main floor, is the fourth bedroom usable or a closet with ambition. Without a floor plan, some of them book a showing just to find out, and leave in nine minutes.

That showing looks like activity. It isn't. It's you cleaning the house and leaving for an hour so someone can learn what a drawing would have told them. The floor plan trades those away for the buyers who were scrolling past because they couldn't tell how the house worked.

Judging the Work Before You Hire

Ask for two or three complete recent listings from a photographer, not a highlight reel. A portfolio is the best frames from a hundred shoots. A full listing is what you're actually buying.

Look at the sequence: does it walk the house the way a person would move through it, or jump from the kitchen to a bedroom to the exterior and back? Look at consistency — are the whites the same room to room, are the verticals straight, do the windows show what's outside or blow out to white? In a valley where the view out the window is often the reason someone buys, blown-out windows are a real loss.

And look at the ordinary houses in their portfolio, not the architectural ones. Anyone can photograph a new build on Whitefish Lake. What matters is what they did with a well-kept 1994 ranch on a normal street — that's the assignment most of the time.

The Question Worth Sitting With

Pull up your own listing on your phone, or a neighbor's if you aren't listed yet. Scroll it the way a stranger would — fast, unimpressed, with four other tabs open.

Does it hold you? Or does your eye slide off it?

That's the whole test, and you already know the answer.

item.title: The 90-Day Listings: What Aging Inventory Is Telling Flathead Sellers
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Most sellers ask how the Flathead market is doing. The more useful question is how homes listed 90-plus days ago are doing compared to homes listed in the last 30 — because that spread tells you whether it's the market or your price.
item.content:encoded:
It's Labor Day. By tomorrow morning the valley goes back to work, the summer lookers are gone, and what's left on the market is what's actually for sale.

So here's the question worth asking before you do anything else with your listing this week: when your house doesn't sell, how do you know whether that's the market or your price?

Most sellers never separate those two things. They read a headline about inventory or rates, decide the whole valley is slow, and settle in to wait. Sometimes that's right. Often it isn't — and the difference is expensive.

Numbers first, then the read.

The Numbers: The Month That Just Ended

Kalispell, for the period August 6 through September 6, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, that period):

  • Active inventory: 504 properties, down 2.33% from the prior month
  • New listings: 96, down 8.57%
  • Average days on market, active listings: 116.67 days, up 12.18%
  • Price changes: 160 listings adjusted price, up 68.42%
  • Average list price, active inventory: $982,000, up 4.92%
  • Asking price per square foot on new listings: $419, up 19.42%

Whitefish, same period, same source: 300 active properties, down 4.15%. New listings 52, down 11.86%. Average days on market 152, up 10.96%. Price changes 46, down 22.03%. Average asking price about $2.5 million.

Rates. The Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.71% for the week of September 3, 2026 — up from 6.66% the week before, with the 15-year at 6.04%. A year ago the 30-year averaged 6.50% (source: Freddie Mac PMMS, September 3, 2026).

One note on the regional monthly figures: the Northwest Montana Association of REALTORS® county-level report still stops at July 2026. The August numbers land mid-September. So the freshest picture available today is the MLS activity above.

Read the Average Again

116.67 days is the average for active Kalispell listings. Not sold. Active. Still sitting.

That is the number most sellers skip past, and it reframes everything. When the average unsold home in Kalispell has been on the market nearly four months, the 90-day listing isn't the sad outlier at the end of the row. The 90-day listing is the market. Whitefish is further out still, at 152 days.

Which means the comparison a seller actually needs isn't their house against "the valley." It's their house against two very different groups sharing the same MLS.

The Two Cohorts Nobody Separates

The aged group has been out there since roughly May or June. They've had the showings. They've had the feedback. And 160 of them adjusted price in the last thirty days — against 504 active listings, that's close to one in three cutting inside a single month, at a pace 68% higher than the month before. That group is no longer guessing what the market will pay. It's finding out, in public, one reduction at a time.

The new group is the 96 listings that came on in the last month — and they came on asking 19.4% more per square foot than the prior month's new listings did.

Sit with that for a second. The homes that have been tested are cutting. The homes that haven't been tested are entering higher. Every new seller in Kalispell right now is pricing against the summer they hoped for, while their competition down the street is pricing against the summer that actually happened.

That gap closes exactly one way, and it isn't the aged listings coming back up.

Whitefish Is Playing a Different Hand

Whitefish sellers sat longer — 152 days on average — and adjusted less, with price changes down 22%. Higher-end and second-home sellers usually have the balance sheet to wait, and many are choosing to. That's a legitimate strategy when there's no clock on you.

It is not a strategy that transfers. If you have a payment, a move, a job start, or a decree with a date on it, "wait it out" is borrowing from a future you haven't budgeted for. Carrying a Kalispell house through a Montana winter has a real monthly cost, and it doesn't pause because the listing does.

What This Means Before Rates Come Up

They won't rescue you. 6.71%, five basis points higher than last week and twenty-one basis points above last September. Rates have been flat-to-slightly-up all summer, and if they do fall, they fall for every buyer and every waiting seller on the same morning — which puts you in a bigger crowd, not a better position.

The price you negotiate in a quiet October is permanent. The rate is the part that can be refinanced. Sellers have that backwards more often than not.

The Bottom Line

If your home has been listed 90-plus days in the Flathead, you're in the largest cohort on the board, not a failing minority — and that's genuinely useful information, because it tells you the answer isn't panic.

But it also removes an excuse. When the average active listing is at 116 days and a third of them cut price last month, "the market is slow" stops explaining why the house three streets over went under contract in three weeks and yours didn't.

So the honest question for this week: do you actually know how your list price compares to what closed near you in the last 60 days — not what's asking, what closed? And if you found out today that you were 6% high, would you rather learn it now, in September, or in February after two more reductions?

item.title: Slow Is Smooth, Smooth Is Fast: How Deals Close on Time
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: The fastest outcome almost never comes from the fastest movement. Here's what rehearsed sequence looks like inside a real estate transaction — and why my clients experience it as a deal that never felt rushed and still closed on time.
item.content:encoded:
Slow Is Smooth, Smooth Is Fast: How Deals Close on Time

Think back to the last time you watched somebody handle a genuine emergency well. Not competently — well. What did they actually look like?

Almost nobody describes speed. They describe the opposite. They say the person seemed unhurried. That they moved deliberately while everyone else moved a lot. And then, somehow, the thing was handled before anyone else had finished deciding what to do.

That gap between how it looked and how fast it went is the subject of this piece. It isn't a personality trait, and it isn't calm under pressure in the way people usually mean it. It's rehearsal — and it applies to a real estate closing more directly than most people would guess.

The phrase is about sequence, not pace

"Slow is smooth, smooth is fast" gets repeated until it sounds like something printed on a gym wall.

The actual meaning is narrower and more useful. The time cost in almost any complicated process isn't the time spent doing the steps. It's the time spent redoing them. Work that gets done out of order, or done before the information that governs it arrives, gets done twice. Twice is what costs you the calendar. So you move at the pace where you don't have to repeat yourself, and that pace turns out to be faster end to end than the frantic version — not because slow is inherently better, but because smooth eliminates the rework.

The condition that makes it possible is knowing the next three steps before the current one finishes. Not improvising the next step when you get there. Knowing it already, so the moment the current step lands, the following one is already staged.

What that looks like inside a transaction

A residential purchase in the Flathead Valley is a chain of dependencies with a contractual clock running on nearly every link. Most of the pain I see in transactions that go sideways isn't caused by a bad inspection or a difficult appraisal. It's caused by a step that started late because it was waiting on a step that nobody had staged.

So the sequence gets built up front, the day the contract is signed, not the week a deadline gets close.

The deadline calendar comes first. Every date in the contract — inspection, financing, appraisal, title objection, closing — goes on a working calendar with an internal target several days ahead of the contractual one, because a deadline you hit on the last afternoon is a deadline you had no margin on.

The lender conversation happens before the appraisal is ordered, not after it comes back low. I want to know what the file looks like, what documentation is still outstanding, and what the underwriter is likely to question, while there's still room to do something about it.

The repair addendum gets drafted in outline before the inspection report lands. I don't know yet what will be in the report. I do know the shape of the response, who has to sign it, what the deadline is, and what the seller's likely positions are. When the report arrives, we're editing, not starting.

Vendors get lined up before they're needed. In a valley where a good roofer or septic contractor can be booked out for weeks, the difference between "I'll start calling around" and "I called last Tuesday, they can be there Thursday" is often the difference between closing on time and asking for an extension.

None of that is dramatic. That's the point. It's unremarkable work done early, in a window the client never sees.

Why hurry is the expensive option

Here's the part that's counterintuitive for sellers especially, because the pressure to move fast usually feels like the responsible instinct.

Rushed sequence produces rework, and rework in a transaction is not free. It costs a re-negotiation, an extension, a second inspection, a repriced listing, or — in the worst version — a buyer who walks and a property that goes back on market with days-on-market history attached to it. Every one of those is more expensive in time than the deliberate version would have been, and several of them are expensive in money too.

The other cost is judgment. When you're behind, you make decisions on a compressed clock with incomplete information, and in a negotiation the party operating on a compressed clock is the party that concedes. Margin isn't just comfort. It's leverage.

What you'd actually notice as a client

Very little, and that's how it should be. You don't see the calendar, the lender call, or the addendum outline sitting in a folder waiting for a report that hasn't come yet.

What you notice is that nobody ever called you in a panic. That when the inspection report landed with three real issues in it, the response came back the same day and it was already organized. That the closing date on the contract turned out to be the date you actually closed. That the whole thing felt, in retrospect, like less of an ordeal than everyone warned you it would be.

Clients almost never describe that as competence. They describe it as calm. It isn't calm. It's preparation that happened weeks earlier.

The question worth sitting with

If you're about to hire someone for a transaction that matters — and more so if your situation has a complication in it, a timeline that isn't flexible, a second party who has to agree, an estate or a divorce in the background — the question isn't whether they seem sharp in a listing appointment. Almost everyone does.

The question is what already exists on paper before anything goes wrong. Ask what the first week looks like. Ask what gets scheduled the day the contract is signed. The answer tells you whether you're hiring rehearsal or improvisation.

item.title: The Pre-Listing Inspection: Finding It Before the Buyer Does
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: What a pre-listing inspection costs against what a mid-transaction repair request costs, how to triage findings into fix, price it in, or disclose — and why trying to fix everything is almost always the wrong call for Flathead Valley sellers.
item.content:encoded:
Would you rather find out about your roof now, or three days into a buyer's inspection period?

Same roof. Same shingles. Same amount of life left in them. But those are two completely different conversations, and the difference has almost nothing to do with the roof.

In the first one, you have time. You can get three bids. You can decide the repair isn't worth making and adjust your number instead. You can do nothing at all and say so up front.

In the second one, you're under contract. There's a repair request already drafted, a deadline attached to it, and a buyer who was handed a forty-page document full of red text this morning. Whatever you decide now, you're deciding it fast, with the leverage sitting across the table.

Most sellers in Kalispell and Whitefish end up in the second conversation — not because they were hiding anything, but because nobody suggested the first one.

The Arithmetic Most Sellers Never Run

A pre-listing inspection runs a few hundred dollars for a standard single-family home in the valley. More if the house is large, if there are outbuildings, or if you add a separate well and septic evaluation — which, out on acreage here, you generally should.

Now price the alternative.

A mid-transaction repair request is rarely a bill for the actual repair. It's a bill for the repair plus the buyer's uncertainty. Someone reading "roof at end of service life" with no bid attached doesn't imagine the modest fix. They imagine the whole roof — and ask for the whole roof, because their agent has no reason to ask for less.

Then there's the contractor problem, which is specific to where we live. Getting a roofer out on your own timeline in April is a phone call. Getting one inside a ten-day response window in November, when everybody is trying to beat the weather, means taking whoever is available at whatever they quote. You're shopping without the ability to walk away.

Set a few hundred dollars against those two and it stops being a close call.

Triage: Fix It, Price It In, or Disclose and Move On

Here's where people get it backwards. They order the inspection, open the report, count thirty-one flagged items, and panic.

Thirty-one items is a normal report. On a 1998 house with a crawlspace, it's a good one. Inspectors flag everything they see, including things that are simply how the house was built. The report isn't a to-do list — it's raw intelligence, and it needs sorting into three piles.

Fix it. Cheap, fast, and disproportionately alarming to read. Missing GFCI outlets. A loose handrail. A dryer vent running into the crawlspace. Improper clearance around the wood stove. None is expensive, and every one makes a buyer's inspector write a sentence that sounds worse than the problem is. You're not buying the repair — you're buying the absence of the sentence.

Price it in. Real money, real remaining life, no emergency. The roof with five or six years left. The furnace that works fine and is nineteen years old. The septic that passed but is at the age where a buyer starts doing math. You don't have to replace these — you have to be honest about them and let your number reflect them, with a written bid attached so the buyer reacts to a real figure instead of an imagined one.

Disclose and move on. Conditions that are permanent or simply characteristic of the house. The slope of the lot. The original single-pane window in the stairwell. The crawlspace you can't stand up in. These aren't problems to solve. They're facts about the property, and the right buyer accepts them.

The skill isn't in the fixing. It's in the sorting.

Why Fixing Everything Is the Wrong Call

Sellers who try to clear all thirty-one items usually spend more than the market gives back, and often spend it in the wrong places.

Buyers here don't pay a premium for a house with no deficiencies. They pay for the house — the light, the land, the view of the Swan Range, the shop, the fact that it's eleven minutes from the resort. A spotless report doesn't move the number much. A bad surprise costs you leverage at the moment you have the least of it.

There's a sequencing reason too. Every dollar you spend before listing is a dollar you can't put toward a price adjustment later if the market asks for one.

Once You Know, You Know

A fair objection comes up here: if I don't inspect, I don't know, and if I don't know, I don't have to disclose it.

Montana expects sellers to disclose material defects they're aware of, and your broker carries obligations of their own. But the instinct doesn't survive contact with reality, because the buyer is hiring an inspector regardless. The defect gets found either way. The only variable is whether it's found while you control the response or while they do.

Willful ignorance buys you nothing but a worse version of the same day. Confirm your specific disclosure obligations with your broker and your attorney — that's their call, not mine.

The Report Becomes the Argument

Used well, the report stops being a liability and turns into an asset. When you hand a serious buyer a report you commissioned, with the small items already corrected and written bids attached to the larger ones, you've changed what you're selling. You're not asking them to trust the house is sound. You're showing them. A buyer who isn't worried about what's behind the walls negotiates on price alone — a negotiation you can prepare for.

Their inspector will still come, as they should. But when their report says what yours already said, there's nothing to renegotiate.

The Question Worth Sitting With

If you listed this month and a buyer's inspector walked your house on the fifteenth, what would he find that you'd rather have known about in advance?

Most sellers can name it immediately. There's usually one thing — the crawlspace, the roof, the panel, the drainage on the north side — that's been in the back of your mind for a year or two. That instinct is almost always right, and it's the cheapest thing in the process to check.

item.title: Columbia Falls and the Canyon: Glacier's Side of the Valley
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: An amenities-first look at Columbia Falls and the US-2 canyon corridor toward Glacier — commute realities, what's open year-round versus seasonally, how Glacier access changed in 2026, and how the housing stock differs from the Whitefish core.
item.content:encoded:
Most people meet Columbia Falls at about 45 miles an hour.

It's the last real town before the park. You come up from Kalispell, the highway bends east, and twenty minutes later you're at the West Glacier entrance arch. It was the gas stop.

Ask those same people six months later where they'd actually want to live, and a surprising number of them come back to it.

Here's the honest look at the Glacier side of the valley — the town, the canyon above it, and what living out here costs you in drive time.

The Drive Is the Whole Argument

Start with the map — it's the part you can't renovate.

Columbia Falls sits at the hinge of the valley. Kalispell is roughly fifteen minutes down US-2. Whitefish is about twenty minutes north. Glacier Park International Airport is close enough to matter if you travel for work. West Glacier is twenty-odd minutes east.

That combination is unusual. Most of the valley makes you choose between town and the park; Columbia Falls mostly doesn't — Whitefish Mountain Resort is under half an hour, and the Middle Fork put-ins are closer.

The tradeoff is that you're on US-2 for most of it, and US-2 in February is a different road than US-2 in July.

What People Mean by "The Canyon"

Past Columbia Falls the valley narrows into Bad Rock Canyon and the character changes fast.

Hungry Horse, Martin City, and Coram string out along the highway toward the park entrance. Above them, Hungry Horse Reservoir runs south for miles behind the dam — a lot of water, a lot of forest road, and far fewer people than Flathead Lake on an August Saturday. The Middle Fork of the Flathead runs alongside the highway the whole way up; that's the rafting corridor, and the outfitters cluster along it.

Then there's the North Fork Road, running north out of town toward Polebridge and the park's remote western boundary. It is largely unpaved, washboarded by mid-summer, and it is not a commute. Buyers looking up there need to treat power, plowing, and year-round access as real questions, not details.

One direction you're looking at Big Mountain. The other, the Bob Marshall. That's the appeal, and it isn't subtle.

Glacier Access Changed This Year

If your interest here is partly about the park, 2026 is worth understanding, because the rules moved.

The Park Service confirmed in February that vehicle reservations are not required anywhere in Glacier for 2026 — not on Going-to-the-Sun Road, not at Many Glacier, Two Medicine, or the North Fork (National Park Service, "Vehicle Reservations in 2026," page updated June 2026; Hungry Horse News, February 18, 2026).

What replaced them is narrower. Since July 1, private vehicle parking at Logan Pass has been capped at three hours to force turnover. Express shuttles run to Logan Pass from the Apgar Transit Center and Lake McDonald Lodge, ticketed through Recreation.gov at a dollar a head.

For a visitor that's trip-planning trivia. For someone who lives here it's the real difference: you go on a Tuesday morning in late September, not a Saturday in July. Proximity doesn't buy access on demand. It buys the ability to go when everyone else can't.

Going-to-the-Sun's alpine section closes with the first serious snow each fall. Locals plan around that date the way other places plan around a holiday.

What's Open in February

This is what separates people who visit from people who stay.

Columbia Falls carries a real year-round downtown along Nucleus Avenue — restaurants, a brewery, the everyday businesses — plus a full grocery store and its own school district. Meadow Lake Resort sits just outside town with golf and lodging.

The seasonal layer is thinner than summer suggests. The waterpark, many outfitters, and much of the tourist economy above town run on a warm-weather schedule. Come November, the canyon quiets down hard.

Whether that reads as peace or isolation is personal. If you're buying off a July visit, come back in February. I've watched more than one buyer fall for a season instead of a place.

On schools: district boundaries out here don't follow city limits or mailing addresses. Verify the district for a specific parcel.

The Housing Stock Is a Different Animal

In town you'll find a grid of older homes from the mill era on real lots, plus newer infill. Prices generally sit below the Whitefish core for comparable square footage — that gap is why many buyers look here at all.

Outside city limits it changes again: acreage, well and septic instead of city services, longer driveways, and plowing that's yours to solve.

If you're coming from a city, well and septic due diligence is where these deals most often go sideways. Test it, scope it, and get the records before you're emotionally committed to the view.

The Thing Nobody Mentions on the Tour

Straight talk, because you'll find it eventually and I'd rather you hear it early: the former aluminum smelter site on the west edge of Columbia Falls is a federal Superfund site.

It's also finally moving. In July 2026, Columbia Falls Aluminum Company reached a cleanup agreement with the EPA valued at roughly $57.6 million, and remediation is proceeding (Flathead Beacon, July 8, 2026; EPA news release).

That's not a reason to avoid the area — thousands of people live here, and the site is contained and monitored. It is a reason to ask specific questions about a parcel's proximity, read the disclosures carefully, and have your own inspector and attorney review anything that concerns you. I'm not an environmental professional or an attorney, and nothing here is legal or environmental advice.

I'd rather tell you about it in the truck than have you find it in a title report.

Is This Actually Your Side of the Valley?

When you picture your Saturday twelve months from now — not the vacation version, the ordinary one — does it start with a trailhead twenty minutes away and end with a quiet town? Or does it need a walkable downtown with something happening in it?

Both answers are correct. They just point at different parts of the Flathead, and knowing which one you are saves months of looking at the wrong listings.

item.title: Clearing Out the House: The Part Nobody Plans For
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: The legal side of an estate comes with a checklist. The garage doesn't. A workable sequence for sorting a lifetime of personal property, how estate-sale companies price and charge, and how to time the clear-out against the listing.
item.content:encoded:
Clearing Out the House: The Part Nobody Plans For

The legal side of an estate comes with a checklist. Somebody hands you one — file this, notify these people, open that account.

The garage doesn't come with anything.

In my experience, families almost never stall on the paperwork. They stall in the house. Forty years of things, no order to any of it, and nobody wanting to be the one who throws out something that turns out to have mattered. Months go by that way, and the estate pays for every one of them — taxes, insurance, utilities, a lawn somebody has to mow.

If you can feel that stall coming, here's a sequence that works.

The disclaimer first, and I mean it: I'm a real estate agent, not an attorney. What a personal representative may distribute, sell, or dispose of — and when — depends on the will and on Montana probate rules. Confirm your authority with your attorney before anything leaves the house. What follows is the order of operations, not the law.

Documents and valuables come out first

Before a box gets donated, one person walks the house looking for two things: paper and portable value.

Paper means deeds, titles, insurance policies, tax returns, military discharge records, safe-deposit keys, and the handwritten note in a drawer that turns out to be a codicil. Portable value means jewelry, firearms, coins, cash tucked in books, and anything small enough to disappear during a clear-out without anyone noticing.

Do this early, with a second person present, and put it all in one secured place. Not because anyone in your family is a thief — but because a dozen people are about to move through that house, and the version of this story that ends badly always starts with "we found it later, we think." Firearms have their own transfer rules; ask your attorney before handing one to a nephew.

Then sort into five piles, not two

Families freeze because they sort into "keep" and "toss," forcing an emotional verdict on every object. That's exhausting by lunch. Five categories move faster:

Keep — a specific person has claimed it and will physically carry it out.

Distribute — spoken for, but the person is in Tucson until October. This pile needs a shipping plan or a date, or it becomes a permanent resident.

Sell — real resale value: furniture in good condition, tools, equipment, collections, anything with a brand name people search for.

Donate — usable, but not worth the cost of selling. Most of the house lands here.

Haul — broken, stained, expired, or waterlogged. Be honest about the volume; it's usually a dumpster's worth, and renting one on day one beats eleven trips to the transfer station.

One rule that saves families grief: photograph anything sentimental before it goes. Nobody misses the object as much as not having looked at it one more time.

How estate-sale companies actually work

The economics surprise people, so know them before you call anyone.

An estate-sale company runs the sale in the house over a weekend and takes a percentage of gross proceeds — commonly 30 to 50 percent, depending on the company, the size of the sale, and the labor the setup requires. Many have a minimum in sellable contents before they'll take the job. Ask directly: what's the split, is there a minimum, who handles what doesn't sell, and is there a separate cleanout fee.

Consignment is a different animal — the piece sits on their floor until it sells and you're paid on a delay. Fine for a few valuable items, bad for volume. Auction houses earn a call when there's a real collection. And "buyout" companies offer a flat number for the whole contents and haul it themselves; you'll net less, but when heirs are scattered and the calendar is the real problem, that can be the right trade — just make it knowingly.

Get two opinions before you commit, and get the terms in writing.

When the heirs are in three states

This is the Flathead reality more often than not — one heir here, the others in Seattle and Dallas with a long weekend each.

What works: an inventory before anybody flies in. Walk the house with a phone, photograph rooms and then anything a person might care about, and share the album. Then set a claiming window — everyone marks what they want by a stated date, conflicts resolve by a method agreed on in advance, and silence counts as no claim. Rotating draft picks sounds childish until you watch it end a standoff in twenty minutes.

The visit itself is for goodbyes and boxes. Discovery by group, in person, is how weekends turn into arguments.

Time the clear-out against the listing, not after it

Two failure modes, opposite directions. Photographing a full house and hoping buyers see past it costs real money — clutter reads as a project regardless of the bones. The other extreme is worse than people expect: a house stripped bare in October and listed in February has spent four months empty, aging in the eyes of the market, while the estate pays the carrying costs.

The version that works is staged. Valuables secured. Sale or donation of contents. Broom-clean and light repairs. Photos, then market — the last two close enough together that the house isn't sitting vacant waiting on a photographer.

And you don't have to empty it before I can tell you what it's worth. A walkthrough with the contents still in place is usually more useful — I can see the house instead of imagining it.

The part worth saying out loud

The clear-out is the last thing the family does in that house together. Treat it like it matters — but put a calendar around it, or grief and logistics braid into a project nobody finishes.

So the question worth sitting with: is the hold-up actually the stuff — or that nobody has said out loud what date this needs to be done by?

No pressure toward a listing you're not ready for. item.title: Buying Before the Snow: What to Check on a Flathead Home in September
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: A house shown in September tells you almost nothing about how it lives in February. The roof, attic, heat source and backup, pipe runs, drainage, and the plowing question — here's what to check on a Flathead Valley home while the weather still lets you.
item.content:encoded:
Buying Before the Snow: What to Check on a Flathead Home in September

Here's a question for anyone touring homes in the valley right now: what would this house look like on the second week of January, at ten below, with two feet on the roof?

Because a house shown in September tells you almost nothing about how it lives in February. The lawn is green, the driveway is dry, the furnace hasn't run in months, and every window is open. Everything that makes a Flathead winter easy or miserable is invisible in good weather.

The upside is that September is exactly when you can still get up on the roof, into the crawlspace, and down the road to see what you're buying. That window closes fast. Here's what to check while it's open.

Start With the Roof — and Ask About Ice

Roof age is the first number to get, and "it's fine" is not an answer. Ask for the year it was replaced and who did it. If nobody knows, that's information too.

Then look at the pitch and the eaves. Low-slope roofs and complicated rooflines with valleys and dormers hold snow longer and are more prone to ice damming — that cycle where heat escaping the house melts snow on the roof, it refreezes at the cold eave, and water backs up under the shingles. Evidence of past damming shows up as stained or bubbled ceiling drywall near exterior walls and heat-cable staples along the roof edge. Heat cables aren't a red flag by themselves, but they're a sign someone was managing a problem rather than solving it.

Look at where the downspouts dump, too. Water directed at the foundation is a summer nuisance and a winter wall of ice.

The Attic Is Where Winter Problems Come From

Most ice damming and a lot of heating cost start in the attic, not on the roof. Ask the inspector to actually get in there, not just look through the hatch.

What matters: insulation depth and whether it's even, or whether it's been pushed around and compressed. Whether soffit and ridge vents are present and not buried under insulation. Any sign of moisture — dark staining on the underside of the sheathing, frost residue lines, mold — which points to warm, damp house air getting into a cold attic. Bathroom fans venting into the attic instead of outside are a common find in older valley homes — a cheap fix compared to the sheathing they'll eventually rot.

What Heats It — and What Backs That Up

This is the question I'd push hardest on, and it has two parts: what's the primary heat, and what happens when it fails or when the power goes out on a cold night?

Propane. Ask who owns the tank. A leased tank usually ties you to that supplier and their pricing; an owned tank lets you shop. Ask for fill history so you can see real winter consumption, not a guess. And confirm the tank isn't sitting where the plow will hit it or the roof will dump onto it.

Wood stove. Get the model and the install date, and have the inspector check clearances to combustibles, the hearth, and the chimney. Ask when the chimney was last swept — your insurer will ask about the stove anyway.

Heat pump. Ask specifically whether it's a cold-climate rated unit and what the backup heat source is. Standard air-source heat pumps lose capacity as temperatures fall; a cold-climate model or a strip-heat or furnace backup is what actually carries the house through a January cold snap. If the answer is "the heat pump handles it," ask what the electric bill looked like last February.

Furnace or boiler. Age, last service date, and — for gas — whether there's a carbon monoxide detector on every level.

And for any of the above: is there a generator hookup, or a plan for one?

Where the Pipes Run

Frozen pipes are the winter emergency that costs the most and gets the least attention on a September walkthrough.

The questions: are there water lines running through an unheated crawlspace, garage, or exterior wall? How is the crawlspace insulated, and are the vents closed for winter? Is there heat tape on exposed runs, and does it work? Where's the main shutoff?

A crawlspace with standing water, bare dirt, or daylight showing through the rim joist is telling you something about February.

Grading, Drainage, and the Melt

Snow eventually turns into a lot of water, all at once, usually in March. Walk the perimeter and look at whether the ground slopes away from the foundation or toward it. Look for efflorescence — that white mineral staining — on basement walls, and for a sump pump and whether it has a battery backup. A basement that's dry in September has not yet been tested.

The One Nobody Asks About: Who Plows the Road?

Here's the question that gets skipped until the first storm. If the home is on a private or shared road — and a large share of homes outside the city limits of Kalispell, Whitefish, and Columbia Falls are — find out who plows it, under what agreement, and what it costs.

Ask for the road maintenance agreement in writing. Ask whether a homeowners' or road association collects for it, or whether it's a handshake between neighbors — and what happens if one owner stops paying. Ask how far the county plow actually comes. Then look at the driveway itself: length, slope, and whether there's anywhere to push the snow. A steep, shaded, north-facing driveway is a different winter than a flat one in the sun.

If the answer to all of this is a shrug, price a plow contract before you write the offer.

How to Use This

None of this is a reason not to buy a house here. It's a reason to know what you're buying before you commit — and to write your inspection contingency with enough time to get a roofer or an HVAC tech out if the general inspection raises a flag. Most of these items come back as "fine" or "fixable for a known number." The point is to be the one who knows the number.

So: of the homes on your list right now, which one can you actually picture on a January morning — and which one have you only seen in September?
