item.title: When One Spouse Won't Cooperate with the Sale
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: The decision to sell is made — and one party stops responding. Here's what the process actually looks like when cooperation breaks down in a Flathead Valley divorce sale, and why documenting everything protects the person acting in good faith.
item.content:encoded:
When One Spouse Won't Cooperate with the Sale

The hardest calls I take in this work don't start with a question about price.

They start with some version of this: the decision to sell has already been made — by agreement, by attorneys, or by a judge — and one person has simply stopped participating. Won't sign the listing paperwork. Won't confirm showing times. Won't leave the house for the open house. Answers the attorney but not the agent, or answers neither.

If that's where you are, the first thing worth saying is that this is more common than you'd guess, and it is almost never as unsolvable as it feels at week three.

Non-cooperation usually isn't strategy

It's tempting to read silence as a tactic. Sometimes it is. Far more often it's one of three other things.

It's grief with a deadline attached. For one spouse, listing the house is paperwork. For the other, it's the last physical thing they're being asked to let go of, and every showing is a stranger walking through it. Slowing it down is the only lever left.

It's an information gap. People who haven't seen the numbers assume the worst about them. Someone who genuinely believes they're being rushed into a bad sale will dig in, and from inside that belief, digging in is the reasonable response.

It's a control question, not a house question. When most of a life has been decided by other people over the last year, the calendar of a home sale can become the one thing left to say no to.

None of that excuses a stalled sale. But the response to each is different, and treating all three as bad faith guarantees you get bad faith.

Why your agent has to stay neutral — and what that buys you

If you're the spouse who wants this done, there's a version of this you might want from me: an advocate who works around the other party.

I won't do that, and the reason is practical rather than principled. The moment one spouse decides the agent belongs to the other one, every request I make becomes something to resist. A listing agent perceived as taking sides stops being able to move the transaction at all.

So the protocol is the same in every one of these files. Both parties get the same information at the same time, in the same message. Both attorneys are copied on anything substantive. No side conversations about strategy with either spouse, and I say so out loud to both of you at the start. Price opinions, net sheets, offer summaries, inspection findings — one document, one send, both names on it.

That's not fence-sitting. It's the thing that keeps a reluctant party at the table long enough to sign.

Write the access rules into the listing agreement up front

Most cooperation fights are really scheduling fights, and most scheduling fights are avoidable if the rules get set before the sign goes in the yard.

When one spouse still occupies the home, we put the specifics in writing at listing:

  • Showing windows. Defined blocks — weekday evenings and weekend afternoons, say — rather than open-ended access. A predictable schedule is far easier to agree to than "whenever a buyer asks."
  • Notice required, and how showings get confirmed. A set minimum, one system, both parties notified — so there's never a dispute about whether a request was received.
  • Open house terms. Whether there will be any, and who is responsible for being elsewhere.
  • Photography and marketing. When photos happen and whether personal items are removed first.
  • Occupancy standard. What condition the home is kept in, and who handles it.

Spelling this out at the start converts a series of individual asks — each of which can be refused — into one agreement already made. When a request is later declined, there's an objective standard to point at instead of a personality conflict.

What a Montana court can do — and what your attorney drives

This is the part where I stop and say clearly: I'm not an attorney, nothing here is legal advice, and what gets filed in your case is your attorney's call, not mine.

What I can tell you as the person who works these files is that a district court handling a Montana dissolution has broad authority over the marital estate, including the home. Courts can and do enter orders addressing the sale of a marital residence — how it's listed, that a party sign the necessary documents, that showings be permitted, and in some cases appointing someone to sign on a refusing party's behalf so a closing isn't held hostage.

Whether any of that fits your situation, and whether it's worth the cost and the relationship damage of pursuing, is a conversation for your attorney. Most of the time it doesn't come to that. But it matters that you know the process isn't powerless — because the belief that it is powerless is what makes people accept a stall that's costing them real money.

Document everything, in writing, without exception

If cooperation has broken down, this is the single most useful habit you can adopt today.

Every showing request, every proposed time, every response, every non-response — in writing. Not a message you'll paraphrase later. Not a phone call you remember clearly. Written, dated, and preserved.

Two reasons. First, if your attorney ever does need to show a court a pattern, a clean record of twenty specific declined or ignored requests is a different document than a summary of how the last two months felt.

Second, and more useful day to day: it protects you. Both spouses in a stalled sale usually believe the other one is the obstacle. A written record is the only thing that settles that without a fight — and it's just as capable of showing you were the difficult one as showing you weren't. That's what makes it credible.

On my side, requests go out in writing to both parties and both attorneys, and I keep the timeline. Not to build a case against anyone — because a documented process is a calm process, and calm is the whole job here.

A question worth sitting with

If the sale closed sixty days from now, what would you want the record of these last few weeks to show about how you handled it?

That's usually the more useful question than who's being unreasonable — and it's the one you actually control.

If you're in the middle of this and want a straight read on what's realistic from someone who does this work regularly and takes no side, email me directly at ryan@westcompanies.com, or call the office anytime at (406) 709-5404 — the line is answered day or night, and the conversation stays confidential. No pressure, no obligation, and nothing gets listed because we talked.

item.title: The Fall Window: What September Does to Flathead Prices
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Every seller in the valley has been told to wait for spring. Here's what the September-through-November stretch actually does to Flathead Valley inventory, days on market, and negotiating leverage — and who the fall buyer really is.
item.content:encoded:
If you've had your home on the market this summer and it hasn't sold, somebody has probably already told you the same thing: pull it, wait for spring, relist in April.

Here's the question worth asking before you take that advice: what do you actually believe happens between now and then?

Because the honest answer for most sellers isn't a strategy. It's a hope that a different season will fix a problem that isn't seasonal.

It's Monday. Numbers first, then the read.

The Numbers: Labor Day Week 2026

Kalispell, for the period July 29 through August 29, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, that period):

  • New listings: 100, down 5.7% from the prior month
  • Active inventory: 506 properties, down 1.9%
  • Days on market, active listings: 114, up 9.3%
  • Price changes: 162 listings adjusted their price, up 47.3%
  • Average list price, active inventory: $981,000

Whitefish, for July 30 through August 30, 2026 (same source, Whitefish report): 47 new listings, down 20.3%. Active inventory 298, down 4.8%. Days on market 152, up 10.6%. Average asking price north of $2.3 million.

The wider region. The most recent monthly figures for Flathead, Lincoln, and Lake counties remain July 2026: median sales price $612,500, down 2.8% year over year; 1,479 homes for sale, up 11.5% from July 2025; average days on market 104; sellers receiving 97.3% of asking price (source: Northwest Montana Association of REALTORS®, July 2026 market update, published August 17). The August figures won't publish until mid-September.

Rates. The Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.66% as of August 27, 2026 — up a single basis point from 6.65% the week before, with the 15-year at 5.98% (source: Freddie Mac PMMS, August 27, 2026). A year ago the 30-year averaged 6.56%. Rates are flat and have been flat all summer.

What Fall Actually Does

Let me be straight about what I can and can't prove here. I don't have a clean multi-year study of Flathead September closings to hand you, and I'm not going to invent one. What I can tell you is the mechanism, and you can watch it happen in the numbers above.

Fall doesn't change what buyers will pay. It changes what they're choosing between.

New listings in Kalispell are down again, and down 20% in Whitefish. That decline accelerates through the fall — nobody puts a house on the market Thanksgiving week. Supply thins.

Demand thins too. But it thins differently: it doesn't shrink so much as it concentrates.

The June buyer was often browsing — vacationing, half-looking, curious what a place near the lake runs. The person still touring homes the second week of November is not browsing. They have a start date, a closing on the other end, a lease expiring, or a reason they can't wait until spring.

So the ratio moves. Fewer houses competing, and the shoppers who remain are disproportionately the serious ones. That's the fall window. It isn't a price rally. It's a change in who's in the room.

The Number That Should Actually Worry You

One hundred sixty-two price changes in Kalispell in a single month, up 47%.

That is nearly a third of all active inventory adjusting its number in thirty days. And notice it's happening while inventory is shrinking — the market isn't correcting because of a supply flood. It's correcting because summer asking prices were ahead of the buyers.

If your home is sitting at or past that 114-day average, you're already in that cohort. You just haven't filed the paperwork.

And here's what "wait for spring" costs you: your listing sits accumulating days on market, or you withdraw and relist later carrying a stale history any decent buyer's agent will pull in about nine seconds. Meanwhile the spring you're waiting for is the season when everyone lists. Your competition in April is every seller who took the same advice you did, plus the natural spring inventory, all at once.

You'd be trading a thin-competition fall for a crowded spring, and paying carrying costs for seven months to do it.

If You're Buying

The leverage is real, and it has an expiration date.

A seller at 114 days who has already cut once — or twice, given those 162 adjustments — is doing math at the kitchen table every night about carrying that house through a Montana winter. That's where concessions live: rate buydowns, closing credits, repair money that simply did not exist in June.

Rates aren't rescuing anyone. 6.66%, one basis point off the prior week, a tenth of a point above last August. If your plan is to wait for cheaper money, understand that cheaper money arrives for everyone simultaneously — and you'll be bidding against every other person who waited. The price you negotiate in a quiet October is permanent. The rate is the part you can refinance.

The Bottom Line

September through November isn't the market's dead zone. It's the market's filtered zone — less competing inventory, fewer casual shoppers, and both sides finally motivated by something more concrete than a season.

What it will not do is rescue a price the summer already rejected. A home priced to what closed nearby in the last 60 days sells this fall. A home priced to June's optimism sits until it becomes the 163rd price change.

So the question worth sitting with this week: if you're selling, is "wait for spring" an actual plan — or is it just the least uncomfortable thing to do with a listing that hasn't sold? And if you're buying, which of those 114-day Kalispell listings would you look at differently knowing the seller is now staring at a winter of carrying costs?

item.title: First Light: Why the Day Starts Before the Day Starts
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: I'm up and working before the Flathead Valley wakes up, and it has almost nothing to do with fitness. Here's what the hours nobody watches actually buy — and why my clients feel it as calm.
item.content:encoded:
First Light: Why the Day Starts Before the Day Starts

Here's a question worth asking about anyone you're thinking of hiring: what were they doing three hours before you called them?

Not in a nosy way. In a practical one. Because by the time you pick up the phone with a real question — an offer deadline, an inspection report that just landed, a lender who's gone quiet — the answer you get is already mostly determined. It was set hours earlier, in a window you'll never see.

I'm usually up and working before the valley is. Long before it, most days. People assume that's a fitness thing. The training is in there, and I do care about it. But it isn't the reason, and it never was.

What the early hours were actually for

In the Army, and later in protective services work for the US government, the day got won or lost in the hours nobody watched.

Gear laid out the night before, then checked again cold, because the version of you at 0400 is not the version of you who packed at 2200. The route walked in your head twice — not the route as drawn, the route as it would actually go, including the part where it doesn't. The small hard thing done before anybody asked for it.

By the time anything actually happened, most of it had already been handled. That's the whole trick, and it isn't much of a trick. It's just front-loading. You move the thinking to the quiet part of the day so that the loud part of the day only requires execution.

Nobody gives you credit for that block of time. Nobody sees it. If it's done well, the visible part of the day looks almost boring, and that's the goal. Drama in the field usually means somebody skipped the morning.

The part that isn't about fitness

Getting after it before sunrise in a Montana winter — fifteen below, dark, glare ice, no reason on earth to be out there — does not make me a better negotiator. That would be a nice story. It isn't true.

What it does is smaller and more useful. It settles the question of whether the day happens on my terms. By the time the sun comes up over the Swan Range, I've already done one thing I didn't feel like doing. The rest of the day is negotiating with someone who's already won the first argument.

That's the entire crossover. Anybody who tells you cold-water discipline translates directly into deal-making is selling something.

What actually gets done before the phone rings

Here's the honest inventory of that early block, because "discipline" is a useless word if it doesn't turn into specifics.

Active files get read before anything else. Not skimmed for what's due. Read, looking for what's about to be due, and for the thing that's quietly gone three days without a response. Most transaction problems announce themselves well before they become problems. They just do it in the boring paperwork nobody reads on a Sunday.

Deadlines get walked forward, not backward. Inspection window, financing contingency, appraisal, title commitment, closing date. Which one is closest, who has the ball, and what happens to the other four if that one slips. If a date is going to be tight in nine days, I'd rather know about it this morning than the afternoon it breaks.

The market gets checked while it's quiet. New listings, price changes, what actually went pending overnight and at what number. Aggregated county data is weeks behind by the time it publishes. What sold in Kalispell or Whitefish this week is current, and it's only current if you look at it consistently.

The hard call gets planned. If I owe someone news they won't like — a low appraisal, a repair request that isn't going to fly, a price conversation a seller isn't ready for — I work out how to say it before I'm saying it. Sitting down, on purpose, in the quiet. Bad news delivered well is a different experience than bad news delivered off the cuff, and clients can absolutely tell the difference.

The contingency gets written before it's needed. This is the one that pays. What's plan B if the buyer's financing wobbles, if the inspection turns up something structural, if the other agent goes dark for a week. Not because I expect all of it. Because writing it down takes eleven minutes at six in the morning and takes a deal apart at four in the afternoon.

None of that is impressive. It's a routine. That's precisely why it works — impressive things are hard to repeat, and routines aren't.

Why this is a service standard, not a personality trait

Discipline isn't a virtue I'm claiming here. It's a system I'm describing, and the reason it matters to you is that it separates an agent who's reacting to your transaction from one who's already run it. Anyone can be calm on an easy deal. The question is what happens when your file is the complicated one — a divorce sale where two households have to coordinate, an estate where the heirs live in three states, a closing where something genuinely goes wrong.

In those files, preparation isn't a nicety. It's the entire service.

What my clients experience isn't the early mornings. They never see that part. What they feel is that nothing catches me flat. The question they were nervous to ask has already been answered. When something ugly lands, the response is a procedure instead of a scramble.

That calm isn't temperament. It's the residue of a lot of quiet hours.

The question worth sitting with

If you're weighing who to work with on the biggest transaction of your year — especially if your situation is complicated, because complicated is the file I want — the question isn't whether someone seems confident when you meet them. Everybody seems confident at the listing appointment.

The question is what they'll have already done, three hours before you call with the problem.

item.title: Pricing Into a Slow Market Without Getting Chased Down
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: When roughly one in three Kalispell listings has already cut its price, pricing stops being about optimism and starts being about sequence. Here's how Flathead Valley sellers set a number they can hold.
item.content:encoded:
Pricing Into a Slow Market Without Getting Chased Down

There's a specific kind of misery in a slow market, and most sellers walk into it the same way.

You list high — you can always come down. Two weeks pass with three showings and no offers. You cut ten thousand. Nothing. A month later, fifteen more. By October you're forty thousand below where you started at 140 days on market, and the offers coming in are below your original number minus every cut you've made.

You didn't price the house. You chased the market down a hill.

What the Valley Is Actually Doing

For the period July 23 through August 23, 2026, Kalispell showed 510 active properties and 157 price changes — adjustments up 30.8% from the prior month, on inventory averaging 113 days on market (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, August 2026 period).

Roughly one in three active listings has already reduced.

Here's the part that matters more than the headline: across northwest Montana in July, sellers still received an average of 97.3% of asking price, and closed sales were up 14.9% year over year (source: Northwest Montana Association of REALTORS®, July 2026 market update).

Read those together and they say something precise. Homes are selling, and sellers who close aren't getting gutted at the table. The haircut in this market lands on the listing price — before the sign ever goes up — not on the right price.

The money isn't lost in negotiation. It's lost in the first thirty days, at a number that was never real.

The First Two Weeks Are the Only Honest Feedback You Get

When a home hits the market it gets a burst of attention that never comes back. Every buyer in your price band sees it that week. Every saved search fires. That audience is finite, and it shows up once.

If your number is wrong, they don't argue with you about it — they just don't come. And that's the trap: no showings feels like no information, so sellers wait. It's actually the clearest information you'll ever get.

Three mechanical questions at day 14:

  • How many showings? Under five in two weeks in this market is a price signal, not a marketing problem.
  • Any second visits? Traffic with no repeats usually means your house is the one buyers look at to feel good about something else.
  • What went under contract near you since you listed, and at what number?

Sellers who reprice at day 14 usually reprice once. Sellers who wait until day 60 reprice three times.

What an Aspirational Number Actually Costs

The pitch for pricing high is that it's free. It isn't. It costs you in three places.

Days on market. At 113 days average, you don't have much runway before a listing reads as stale. Buyers watch that number, and a house at 90-plus days invites a lower opening offer than the same house at 20 — usually lower than the reduction you were avoiding.

Position in the search. A $749,000 home listed at $799,000 stops competing with the $749,000 homes and starts losing to the $799,000 ones. Priced right, it's the best house in its bracket. Overpriced, it's the cautionary tale one bracket up.

Your negotiating posture. Every reduction is a public signal. Cut three times and buyers stop asking what the house is worth and start asking how much more you'll take.

The seasonal clock matters too. New listings in Kalispell were down 13.1% last month and inventory thins through fall — a real tailwind for a correctly priced home in September. But a house still chasing a spring number in November enters the slowest stretch of the year with the worst story on the sheet.

A Reset vs. a Follow

Not all reductions are the same, and this is where sellers lose money quietly.

A follow is a small cut to stay just under the last comparable sale. Five thousand off, then five more. Each one keeps you in front of the same buyers who already passed, which is why nothing changes.

A reset is one deliberate move that puts your home in front of a different pool of buyers — under a search threshold, below the listing you keep losing to, at a number that makes your house the obvious value in its bracket. It generates new showings because it reaches people who never saw the listing.

Make it big enough to cross a real threshold: $625,000 to $599,000 reaches an entirely different search than $625,000 to $619,000. Make it once, and time it to a weekend.

One decisive reset almost always nets more than three apologetic ones.

Setting a Number You Can Hold

The number you want is the one you won't be arguing with yourself about in six weeks. That's an exercise, not a feeling.

Start from what's actually closed within about a mile in the last 60 to 90 days — not what's listed, and not what your neighbor turned down in 2023. List prices are opinions. Closings are evidence. Then adjust honestly for what buyers pay for here: usable acreage, view and exposure, garage and shop space, well and septic condition, and how far you sit from a paved road in February.

Run your net sheet before you pick the price, not after you get an offer. If the number that works for your life is above what the comps support, that's worth knowing in August — while timing and prep are still options — rather than in November with three cuts behind you.

Then decide your reset in advance: if we're under X showings with no second visits at day 14, we move to Y, once. Making that call calmly on the front end is a completely different decision than making it at day 45 when the phone has stopped ringing.

Set a real number. Get honest feedback fast. If you have to move, move once and move decisively.

So the question worth sitting with this weekend: do you know what your street has actually closed at in the last 60 days — or is your price built on what you hoped it was worth in the spring?

item.title: September in the Flathead: The Valley's Quietest Month
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: The week after Labor Day, the Flathead Valley changes character — thinner traffic on Highway 93, emptier trailheads, a lake that stays warm long after the crowds go home. What's open, what closes, and why September is the month locals quietly guard.
item.content:encoded:
Ask someone who has lived here a while what their favorite month is, and watch how long they take to answer.

Most of them will tell you. A few will hesitate, because saying it out loud feels like giving something away.

It's September. It's almost always September.

Here's what actually happens, and why it matters if you're thinking about moving to the Flathead Valley — or trying to decide whether the version of this place you saw in July is the real one.

The Week After Labor Day Flips a Switch

Labor Day falls on September 7 this year. The change isn't gradual.

Highway 93 between Kalispell and Whitefish stops feeling like a parking lot. The turn onto Highway 35 toward Bigfork opens back up. Errands that took ninety minutes in August take forty. Restaurant tables in Whitefish and Bigfork — the ones you needed a plan for in July — are available on a Friday.

Trailheads that were full by 7 a.m. have spots at ten. The boat ramps thin out. The line at the hardware store is people you recognize.

Nothing about the valley itself has changed. The seasonal population has, and in a place this size, that's the whole difference.

Glacier in September: What's Open, What Stops

This is where the specifics matter, because the park operates on a calendar and it doesn't care about your weekend plans.

A few things to know for 2026, straight from the National Park Service:

  • Vehicle reservations are not required this year. Glacier dropped the reservation system for 2026 and replaced it with a ticketed-only shuttle to Logan Pass plus three-hour limited timed parking up top.
  • The Logan Pass shuttle runs July 1 through Labor Day, September 7. After that date, the shuttle stops for the season — which means from September 8 on, getting to Logan Pass means driving and parking yourself.
  • The alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road usually stays fully open until the third Monday in October, weather permitting. After that the western gate drops back to Avalanche Creek or Lake McDonald Lodge depending on conditions.
  • Visitor centers close in late September and early October. Most campgrounds close, in-park lodging isn't available in the fall, and Many Glacier Road closes the third weekend in November.

(Source: National Park Service, Glacier National Park planning pages, current as of August 2026. Park operations change — always confirm at nps.gov/glac before you drive out there.)

So the practical picture for mid-September is one of the best trades available anywhere: the road is open, the crowds are gone, the shuttle isn't running, and you can generally park at trailheads that were hopeless six weeks earlier. Bring layers. Logan Pass in late September can be sixty degrees or it can be sleeting sideways, sometimes in the same afternoon.

The Lake Stays Warm Longer Than People Expect

Flathead Lake holds an enormous amount of water, and water gives up heat slowly. The lake doesn't get the memo that summer ended when the calendar says so.

Early and mid-September swimming is normal. The difference is that the bays around Somers, Lakeside, and Bigfork are quiet, the wake traffic drops off, and the light gets low and gold in a way it never does in July. Cherry season has wrapped along the east shore, but the drive is still worth it — arguably more so, without the summer traffic stacked up behind you.

Larch, First Frost, and the Best Air of the Year

Late September is when the western larch start turning up the drainages — the conifer that goes gold and drops its needles, lighting up whole hillsides in a color no other month produces. Peak varies year to year and by elevation; late September into mid-October is the usual window.

You'll notice something else too: the air clears. Late summer in the northern Rockies can mean regional wildfire smoke, and while nothing is guaranteed either way, cooler nights and fall weather patterns tend to move it out. Some of the sharpest, longest views of the year happen in the back half of September.

Mornings get cold. Afternoons stay warm. Bugs are done. Hunting seasons open. If you have a dog, this is the month they'd vote for.

Shoulder Season Cuts Both Ways

Being honest about the tradeoff: some seasonal businesses in the resort-adjacent parts of Whitefish, Bigfork, and Lakeside reduce hours or close entirely between the summer and ski seasons. Scenic lift operations at Whitefish Mountain Resort wind down in the fall. A handful of restaurants take their annual break in October before winter ramps up.

Kalispell — the valley's commercial center, with Logan Health, the airport, and the bulk of the retail — runs year-round and barely notices. But if your picture of living here is built entirely on July, shoulder season is the part of the calendar you haven't met yet.

That's not a warning. It's just the part nobody puts in the listing photos.

If You're Considering a Move, Visit Now — Not in July

The most useful advice I have about relocating here has nothing to do with real estate: come look in September or October.

July shows you the Flathead in costume — every business open, every festival running, the lake full of boats, every hotel charging accordingly. It's a wonderful week, and it tells you almost nothing about a random Tuesday in this valley.

September shows you the drive to work. The grocery store at normal capacity. Which towns still feel alive when the visitors leave and which ones get very quiet. How far things really are from each other when you're not sitting in traffic.

There's a market angle too, and it's simple: the buyers still looking in the fall are generally the serious ones, and the sellers still listed after the summer season are generally the motivated ones. That combination tends to produce more honest negotiations than August does.

The Question Worth Sitting With

So here's what I'd ask if we were having coffee: when you picture living in the Flathead, are you picturing a vacation you had — or a Wednesday in October?

Those are different purchases. One of them is a house. The other is a memory, and a house is an expensive way to buy one.

If you want a straight read on which towns in this valley hold up in the quiet months — and which ones fit how you actually live — I'm glad to walk through it with you, whether you're six weeks or two years out. Email me at ryan@westcompanies.com, or call the office at (406) 709-5404 — the line is answered around the clock. No pitch, no drip campaign. Just a conversation.

item.title: When the Heirs Don't Agree: Selling a Family Home Together
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Most difficult estate sales aren't legally complicated — they're complicated because siblings want different things. What a personal representative can decide alone, how an independent valuation defuses conflict, and how to handle a buyout or a holdout.
item.content:encoded:
When the Heirs Don't Agree: Selling a Family Home Together

The hardest estate sales I've been part of in the Flathead Valley weren't hard for legal reasons. The paperwork was clean. The title was clear. The probate was routine.

They were hard because three siblings wanted three different things, and one of them was living in the house.

If that's the situation you're in — or the one you can feel coming — here's where these go well, and where they go sideways.

First, the disclaimer, and I mean it: I'm a real estate agent, not an attorney. Montana probate has rules about authority, notice, and what a personal representative may do without court involvement, and those rules depend on the will and the specifics of the estate. What follows is meant to help you ask your attorney sharper questions, not to replace the answer.

Name what each person actually wants

Before anyone argues about price, get clear that the disagreement usually isn't about the house at all.

One heir wants the money, often on a timeline. One wants to keep the place in the family — it's where Thanksgiving happened. One is exhausted and wants it over with. And sometimes one is living there, has been for years, and is quietly afraid of being told to leave a home they've been maintaining.

That's four different problems getting treated as one argument about a listing price, which is exactly why the argument never resolves. Put the wants on the table plainly — money, memory, speed, shelter — and stop pretending everyone is negotiating the same point. You can build a plan around four stated needs. You can't build one around a fight.

What the personal representative can and can't decide alone

This question produces the most tension and the most misinformation.

In broad terms, the personal representative carries a legal duty to the estate and to all the beneficiaries — not to whichever heir calls most often. That duty runs both directions: it gives the PR real authority to act, and it obligates them to act in the estate's interest rather than their own.

What that authority covers in practice — whether the home can be listed without every heir signing, what notice the other beneficiaries are owed, whether court approval is required — depends on the will, the type of probate, and the facts of the estate. Ask your attorney to spell it out in writing, early. A PR who knows the boundary of their own authority decides calmly. One who doesn't tends to either overstep or freeze, and both create resentment that outlasts the sale.

That duty also means preserving the estate's value. A house sitting empty through a Flathead winter, unheated and underinsured, isn't a neutral choice.

An independent valuation ends more arguments than any conversation

Here's the single most effective de-escalation tool in an estate sale: get a number from someone who has nothing to gain.

When value is a matter of opinion, every opinion is suspect. The sibling who wants to sell is accused of lowballing. The one who wants to buy the others out is accused of grabbing a bargain. The one out of state has a Zestimate and a theory. Nobody trusts anyone.

A licensed appraisal — often the date-of-death appraisal the estate needs for tax purposes anyway — replaces all of that with a document. Appraised value and market value answer slightly different questions, so it isn't the last word. But it's neutral, it's defensible, and it moves the conversation from "you're trying to cheat me" to "here's the number — now what do we do about it."

Get it early, before positions harden. It costs a few hundred dollars and routinely saves families five figures in legal fees, plus something more expensive than that.

When one heir wants to buy the others out

This is common, and often the right outcome. It usually fails for one of three reasons.

The number was never independently set. A buyout priced by argument is a buyout that gets relitigated later.

Financing wasn't confirmed first. An heir who intends to buy the others out needs to know what they can actually qualify for, and lenders treat estate and probate situations with their own requirements. Answer that in week one, not in month five after everyone has emotionally committed.

Nobody wrote down a deadline. The family that agrees "he'll buy us out when he can" is the family still arguing two years later.

A workable buyout has three things in writing: an independent value, a confirmed source of funds, and a date by which it closes or the house goes to market. Have your attorney paper it.

When someone simply won't sign

Sometimes it isn't obstruction. It's grief wearing the costume of obstruction — the person who won't sign is often the one who isn't ready to close the door on their parents' house, and pressure doesn't fix that.

Slow down enough to find out which one it is. If it's grief, a date on the calendar a few weeks out does more than an ultimatum. If it's a genuine deadlock, that's where your attorney explains the options the estate actually has — worth understanding before anyone makes a threat they'd rather not carry out.

What I'd guard against is letting a deadlock run indefinitely. Every month the estate carries a house nobody is using, it pays for the privilege — taxes, insurance, utilities, upkeep — out of the same pot everyone is arguing over.

Set the timeline before you need it

Almost every estate sale I've seen go smoothly had one thing in common: someone wrote down the phases early and shared them with everyone. Valuation by this date. Buyout decision by this one. Contents cleared by this one, with a stated process for who claims what. On market by this date if the buyout hasn't closed. Nothing dramatic — just a plan, visible to all parties, so nobody has to guess what happens next.

That's the piece I bring to these. In the Army and in the work that followed, the plan wasn't optional and the briefing wasn't a formality — everyone knew the phases, the roles, and what triggered the next move. Families in the middle of a loss don't need a salesperson. They need someone who holds the timeline steady while they handle the harder part.

So here's the question worth sitting with: is your family actually disagreeing about the house — or about four different things nobody has said out loud yet?

If you're a personal representative or an heir trying to get your footing on a Flathead Valley property, I'm glad to talk through the real estate side while your attorney handles the law. I don't take sides between heirs, and I won't push you toward a listing you're not ready for. item.title: Buying Land in the Flathead: What to Check Before the View
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Buying raw land in the Flathead Valley? Access, zoning, water rights, septic suitability, utilities, and floodplain — the due diligence checklist to work through before you fall in love with the view.
item.content:encoded:
Buying Land in the Flathead: What to Check Before the View

Here's a question worth asking before you make an offer on that parcel: if you couldn't see it — if all you had was the paperwork — would you still buy it?

Because land is the one purchase where the listing photos tell you almost nothing. A house shows you its problems eventually — a roof leaks, an inspector writes it all down. Twenty acres with a view of the Swan Range shows you exactly one thing: a view of the Swan Range. Everything that determines whether you can build on it is invisible, and most of it lives in a county file, a state database, or three feet underground.

I've watched buyers fall for a parcel in ninety seconds, then spend a year finding out what they bought. Here's the reconnaissance to run first.

Access Comes Before the View

The first question is the least romantic one: can you legally and physically get to it?

Those are two different questions, and buyers routinely confuse them. Physical access means a driveable route exists. Legal access means you have a recorded, permanent right to use it — an easement that runs with the land and shows up in a title search.

"The neighbor's always let us drive through" is not legal access. That's a favor, and favors end when the neighbor sells.

So pull the title commitment early and read the easements. Find out who maintains the road and whether there's a written maintenance agreement — a shared gravel road with no agreement and six owners becomes its own small war every spring. Ask whether the county plows it. Most rural roads out here, they don't.

And if a parcel touches state trust land, public ownership next door is not the same as a right to cross it.

Zoning: What You're Actually Allowed to Build

Not all of Flathead County is zoned, and that surprises people in both directions — some assume everything is regulated, others that nothing is.

Zoning outside city limits runs through the Flathead County Planning and Zoning Office, and you can pull a parcel's zoning district yourself on the county's interactive mapping site — search by address, owner, or assessor number and open the Parcel Information Report. Inside Kalispell, Whitefish, or Columbia Falls city limits, that city's planning office governs instead.

What you're looking for: the zoning district, minimum lot size, setbacks, and whether what you have in mind — a shop, a guest house, a short-term rental, an ag use, a home business — is permitted outright or needs a conditional use permit.

The county also has a Planner on Duty for short walk-in questions on weekdays — a free, underused resource, and one conversation there can save you an expensive assumption.

Check covenants, too. A subdivision's CCRs can be stricter than county zoning, and they're enforced by neighbors rather than a department.

Water — And the Rule That Changed This Year

No municipal water means you're drilling a well, and Montana's rules changed recently enough that even people who bought land here five years ago are working off stale information.

The framework: small groundwater developments — 35 gallons per minute or less, up to 10 acre-feet per year — qualify for an exception to water-rights permitting and receive a Groundwater Certificate rather than a permit. But under the combined appropriation rule, two or more wells drawing from the same source and exceeding 10 acre-feet together need a permit regardless of flow rate. A 2024 district court decision in the Horse Creek Hills case tightened how that applies to phased subdivisions.

The newer change: under House Bill 681, effective January 1, 2026, you must file a Notice of Intent with DNRC before developing an exempt well, with the department reviewing within ten business days. Authorized notices expire after five years, with one possible five-year extension.

The framework is also actively contested in ongoing litigation, so verify current requirements with DNRC directly rather than relying on any article, including this one. I'm a real estate agent, not a water-rights attorney. If water is central to your plans, talk to one.

Practically: ask what neighboring wells produce and how deep they had to go. The Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology's GWIC database is free and public, and nearby well logs are the best preview of what you'll hit.

Septic, Soils, and the Last Half Mile of Utilities

No sewer means a septic system, and not every piece of ground will take one.

Septic permitting in this county runs through the Flathead City-County Health Department, and approval depends on soil conditions, depth to groundwater, separation from wells and surface water, and system size. The test is a soil evaluation on the actual parcel — not a guess from the road.

Get it scheduled during due diligence, not after closing. A parcel that won't perc is one you can't build on the way you imagined — a price conversation at best.

Then price the utilities. Ask the electric provider what a service extension to your building site costs — power at the property line and power at the far corner of an eighty are very different numbers, sometimes tens of thousands apart. Ask the same about fiber if you work from home, and confirm a propane truck can reach the site in winter.

Finally, check FEMA floodplain mapping and the National Wetlands Inventory before planning a building envelope. Wetlands don't always look like wetlands in August. Look at wildfire exposure honestly too — defensible space, a second way out, and what insurance will cost. In this valley, insurability is part of buildability.

Give the Due Diligence Window Room to Breathe

None of this fits in a ten-day inspection period.

Soil evaluations, title review, county conversations, utility quotes, and a survey take weeks, and in the busy season every inspector and excavator in the valley is booked out. Build the timeline into the offer, so your contingency covers the work instead of expiring in the middle of it.

That's how I brief every land buyer: know the terrain before you commit. For contract language, consult your attorney.

Before You Fall in Love With the View

So here's the question to sit with: on the parcel you're considering, could you answer access, zoning, water, septic, and utilities with evidence — not with what the listing says?

If any one of those is a shrug, that's the conversation to have before you're under contract. No pressure, no obligation.
